title: Clarify first: turn a vague prompt into a precise one
intro: Strong candidates ask before they code. Watch a vague prompt get sharper with each question.

predict.question: The interviewer gives a short, vague problem. What is the best first move?
options: Start coding the first idea you have
Ask about input size, edge cases and expected output
Stay silent and think for ten minutes
predict.reveal: Asking. Size, edge cases and output change which solution is right, and it shows the interviewer how you think.

takeaway: Before coding, ask about input size and range, edge cases and expected output, then restate the problem.

steps.say: The interviewer says: 'Find the duplicates in a list.' It sounds easy, but it is vague. Do not start coding. Ask first.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Size and range: unknown.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

steps.say: Ask about input: 'How many items, and what values?' The answer: up to 100,000 integers, each from 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

steps.say: That answer shapes the plan. 100,000 items rules out checking every pair, and a small value range even allows a counting array.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

steps.say: Ask about edge cases: 'What if the list is empty, has one item, or every value is the same?' Edge cases are where bugs hide.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Empty list? One item? All the same value?

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

steps.say: Agree on the answers out loud: an empty list or a single item has no duplicates, and a value repeated many times is reported once.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Empty or one item: return nothing. All same: report once.

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Unknown. Ask!

steps.say: Ask about output: 'Should I return each duplicate once or every copy? A list, or just true or false?' Answer: each once, any order.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Find the duplicates in a list.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Empty or one item: return nothing. All same: report once.

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Each repeated value once, in any order, as a list.

steps.say: Now restate it: the vague prompt has become a precise one. Saying it back lets the interviewer correct you before you write a line.

cards.title: Prompt
cards.text: Return each repeated value once, any order, from up to 100,000 ints.

cards.title: Input
cards.text: Up to 100,000 integers, values 1 to 1,000.

cards.title: Edge cases
cards.text: Empty or one item: return nothing. All same: report once.

cards.title: Output
cards.text: Each repeated value once, in any order, as a list.

steps.say: Two minutes of questions kept you from solving the wrong problem. Now a hash set that counts repeats is a confident choice.
